True, nobody will buy the stuff to make gratings. I think the film is light sensitive at around 633 and it can take the kind of spatial frequencies necessary for a hologram. In that sense, "it works". However, I think the sensitivty is much lower than claimed by Liti and I also think, based on what I saw, that the efficency is very low. There have been claims that the hologram disappeared or that rings have appeared on the image after exposure. This implies, to me, that the film is seperating from the base. So it would appear that the optical properties of the film is not the only problem, mechanical problems have reared. So, it's not an easy "plug'n'play" kind of material that Liti seems to imply. Certainly I don't believe it can be used by a beginner. In that sense I agree with (and like the phrase) Bob's "hobby killer". Luckily, today's hobbyists have this forum. In the past, beginners have tried to make holograms based on these types of claims and, having failed, think it's their fault. There was no one around to set them straight. Today they can come here.

I don't know if the reflection film is pretty much the same as the transmission film, but i hope Liti have taken into account that efficency is dependant on spatial frequency. If the transmission film has such a low de, I'd hate to think how low the reflection stuff is. It could also be that the film cannot take the higher spatial frequencies.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
At an emulsion thickness of 80 to 100 microns, it may just be too narrow band to see in white light. This makes sense when you say you see it in laser light but not white light. Try a LED. These sort of emulsion depths are usually used for technical holograms or memories, I've never heard of a display piece this deep. 

 For those not aware of it, bandwidth, ie the speread of colours that can diffract off the hologram, is dependant on emulsion thickness. Most display emulsions are of the order of 5 - 15 microns giving a 50nm odd bandwidth (since the entire band of visible light is from 400-700, a 300 nm bandwidth, you're diffracting about 1/6th or approx 20% of the white light). If the bandwidth goes much below 20 microns, there's too little diffracting to see anything in white light. If you like, the smaller the amount of the spectrum that's diffracting, the less the amount of light is coming off the hologram. In my HOE days, I used to get approx 20nm, 10 if I tried hard, with a 40 micron emulsion, which was almost impossible to see in white light. At twice the emulsion depth, the bandwidth could easily be les than 10 nm.
